M., Uszkoreit, J., Le, Q., & Petrov, S. (2019). Natural Questions: A Benchmark for Question Answering Research. Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics.
creator: Tom Kwiatkowski, Jennimaria Palomaki, Olivia Redfield, Michael Collins, Ankur Parikh, Chris Alberti, Danielle Epstein, Illia Polosukhin, Jacob Devlin, Kenton Lee, Kristina Toutanova, Llion Jones, Matthew Kelcey, Ming-Wei Chang, Andrew M. Dai, Jakob Uszkoreit, Quoc Le, Slav Petrov (Google Research)
description: Natural Questions is a question answering dataset pairing real anonymized, aggregated queries issued to the Google search engine with Wikipedia pages from the top 5 search results. Annotators provide long answers (typically paragraphs or other HTML bounding boxes), short answers (entities, spans, or yes/no), or mark the example as having no answer.
name: Natural Questions
rai:annotationsPerItem: Training examples have single annotations; development and test examples have 5-way annotations; a subset of 302 examples was additionally analyzed with 25-way annotations.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The paper reports post hoc evaluation of annotation quality using consensus judgments from four experts and 25-way annotations on 302 examples. Reported precision is 90% for long answers and 84% for short answers, and the paper analyzes variability across annotators.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators worked in three stages: question identification (judge whether the question is good or bad), long answer identification (select the earliest HTML bounding box containing enough information to infer the answer, or mark no answer), and short answer identification (select the answering entity or entities within the long answer, mark yes/no, or mark no short answer). Comprehensive guidelines were developed and annotation quality was constantly monitored.
rai:dataBiases: The paper notes that focusing on Wikipedia may introduce biases, because Wikipedia is only one source of factual information and this source choice may shape the dataset. The authors also note that their heuristics exclude some query types such as shorter queries and "how to" questions.
rai:dataCollection: Questions were sampled from real anonymized, aggregated Google Search queries of 8 words or more that had been issued by multiple users in a short period of time. Heuristics filtered likely questions from the query stream, and questions were kept only if a Wikipedia page appeared in the top 5 Google search results; annotators then labeled question-Wikipedia page pairs.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data sources are real anonymized, aggregated queries issued to the Google search engine and Wikipedia pages returned in the top 5 search results for those queries.
rai:dataCollectionType: User-generated content data, Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is limited to longer queries of 8 words or more, excludes many query types such as "how to" questions, and focuses only on cases where a Wikipedia page appears in the top 5 search results. The authors note that Wikipedia as the sole evidence source may introduce biases, and that answer acceptability can be genuinely ambiguous.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Simple heuristics were used to filter likely questions from the query stream. Questions were retained only when a Wikipedia page appeared in the top 5 Google search results. Part-of-speech tags and entities used in the heuristics were identified with Google's Cloud NLP API.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for question answering research, especially large-scale end-to-end training and evaluation for open-domain QA and natural language understanding.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Google's Cloud NLP API was used to identify part-of-speech tags and entities for the question-filtering heuristics.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset contains real user queries that were anonymized and aggregated before inclusion.
